claim: Animals (metazoans) are not autonomous entities, but rather holobionts composed of the host cell community, various commensal and mutualistic microorganisms, a diversity of parasitic taxa, and in many cases, tumor cells.
source: It is now widely established that animals (metazoans) are not autonomous entities, but rather holobionts composed of the host cell community, various commensal and mutualistic microorganisms, a diversity of parasitic taxa, and in many cases, tumor cells (Ujvari et al., 2016a; Dheilly et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ujvari et al., 2016a and Dheilly et al., 2019, and draws from established scientific consensus.

claim: Parasites and mutualistic organisms have frequently evolved the ability to manipulate the host phenotype (e.g., reproduction, behavior, morphology, physiology, body odor) to favor their transmission and/or survival.
source: While it has been shown that parasites and mutualistic organisms have frequently evolved the ability to manipulate the host phenotype (e.g., reproduction, behavior, morphology, physiology, body odor; Hughes et al., 2012, Johnson and Foster, 2018; Naundrup et al., 2022) to favor their transmission and/or survival, sometimes inducing dramatic alterations (Doherty, 2020), this phenomenon has been poorly investigated in the context of host–tumor interactions.
evidence: Supported by citations to Hughes et al., 2012, Johnson and Foster, 2018, Naundrup et al., 2022, and Doherty, 2020.

claim: Host phenotypic manipulation by parasites has been poorly investigated in the context of host–tumor interactions.
source: While it has been shown that parasites and mutualistic organisms have frequently evolved the ability to manipulate the host phenotype (e.g., reproduction, behavior, morphology, physiology, body odor; Hughes et al., 2012, Johnson and Foster, 2018; Naundrup et al., 2022) to favor their transmission and/or survival, sometimes inducing dramatic alterations (Doherty, 2020), this phenomenon has been poorly investigated in the context of host–tumor interactions.
evidence: Stated as an observation about the state of research in the field.

claim: Malignant cells can manipulate surrounding healthy cells to induce the growth of blood vessels (neoangiogenesis) that bring oxygen and nutrients to the tumor.
source: The only unambiguous evidence of such manipulation is found in the tumoral microenvironment when, for instance, malignant cells manipulate the surrounding healthy cells to induce the growth of blood vessels that bring oxygen and nutrients to the tumor, a process called neoangiogenesis (Hicklin and Ellis, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hicklin and Ellis, 2005, and represents established knowledge about tumor biology.

claim: Evidence regarding the ability of tumor cells to manipulate their host phenotype at levels beyond the tumoral microenvironment is scarce.
source: Evidence regarding the ability of tumor cells to manipulate their host phenotype at other levels is scarce (see Tissot et al., 2016 for a review), and this probably reflects a real rarity of this phenomenon.
evidence: Supported by citation to Tissot et al., 2016 review and represents an assessment of the literature.

claim: Host manipulation capabilities often rely on sophisticated and complex adaptations that evolve during long coevolutionary processes.
source: Indeed, host manipulation capabilities often rely on sophisticated and complex adaptations that evolve during long coevolutionary processes, whereas tumors (neoplasms) most often evolve for only a few years and then die with their host without being able to transmit any acquired traits (Arnal et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Arnal et al., 2015 and represents established understanding of evolutionary processes.

claim: Tumors (neoplasms) most often evolve for only a few years and then die with their host without being able to transmit any acquired traits.
source: Indeed, host manipulation capabilities often rely on sophisticated and complex adaptations that evolve during long coevolutionary processes, whereas tumors (neoplasms) most often evolve for only a few years and then die with their host without being able to transmit any acquired traits (Arnal et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Arnal et al., 2015.

claim: Transmissible tumor cells could more easily evolve manipulative abilities like true parasites.
source: However, like 'true parasites', transmissible tumor cells (vertically – such as in Hydra oligactis [Domazet-Lošo et al., 2014; Boutry et al., 2022b]; or horizontally – such as in Tasmanian devils [Jones et al., 2008]) could more easily evolve manipulative abilities (Tissot et al., 2016; Ujvari et al., 2016b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tissot et al., 2016 and Ujvari et al., 2016b, representing theoretical prediction.

claim: Transmissible tumor cells can be transmitted vertically, such as in Hydra oligactis.
source: However, like 'true parasites', transmissible tumor cells (vertically – such as in Hydra oligactis [Domazet-Lošo et al., 2014; Boutry et al., 2022b]; or horizontally – such as in Tasmanian devils [Jones et al., 2008]) could more easily evolve manipulative abilities (Tissot et al., 2016; Ujvari et al., 2016b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Domazet-Lošo et al., 2014 and Boutry et al., 2022b.

claim: Transmissible tumor cells can be transmitted horizontally, such as in Tasmanian devils.
source: However, like 'true parasites', transmissible tumor cells (vertically – such as in Hydra oligactis [Domazet-Lošo et al., 2014; Boutry et al., 2022b]; or horizontally – such as in Tasmanian devils [Jones et al., 2008]) could more easily evolve manipulative abilities (Tissot et al., 2016; Ujvari et al., 2016b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jones et al., 2008.

claim: There is a lack of evidence that transmissible cancers can manipulate the phenotype of their hosts.
source: Nevertheless, to date, we lack evidence that transmissible cancers can manipulate the phenotype of their hosts.
evidence: Stated as an observation about the current state of knowledge.

claim: Hydra oligactis are cnidarians that frequently develop spontaneous tumors in the lab.
source: Hydra oligactis are cnidarians that frequently develop spontaneous tumors in the lab.
evidence: Stated as an observation about the study organism.

claim: Tumors in Hydra oligactis correspond to abnormal proliferation of germline cells in the hydra's ectoderm.
source: These tumors correspond to abnormal proliferation of germline cells in the hydra's ectoderm (Boutry et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Boutry et al., 2023.

claim: Two hydra lineages harbor neoplasms capable of vertical transmission through buds during asexual reproduction.
source: In 2014, Domazet-Lošo et al., 2014 described a fascinating case of two hydra lineages harboring neoplasms capable of vertical transmission through buds, during the asexual reproduction of hydras.
evidence: Supported by citation to Domazet-Lošo et al., 2014.

claim: Two tumorous hydra lines have been maintained under laboratory conditions for more than 15 years.
source: Thanks to this transmission, these two tumorous hydra lines have been maintained under laboratory conditions for more than 15 years now (Lange, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lange, 2010.

claim: Tumorous hydra polyps have an increased number of tentacles compared to healthy polyps.
source: Beyond the presence of large tumor masses, a curious feature of these hydras is their increased number of tentacles. Specifically, while healthy polyps typically have 6–7 tentacles, tumorous polyps have between 8 and 13 tentacles, even up to 20 (Domazet-Lošo et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Domazet-Lošo et al., 2014.

claim: Healthy hydra polyps typically have 6–7 tentacles.
source: Specifically, while healthy polyps typically have 6–7 tentacles, tumorous polyps have between 8 and 13 tentacles, even up to 20 (Domazet-Lošo et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Domazet-Lošo et al., 2014.

claim: Tumorous hydra polyps have between 8 and 13 tentacles, even up to 20.
source: Specifically, while healthy polyps typically have 6–7 tentacles, tumorous polyps have between 8 and 13 tentacles, even up to 20 (Domazet-Lošo et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Domazet-Lošo et al., 2014.

claim: Tentacle numbers in hydras usually vary in a very small range (from 5 to 8 tentacles, depending on temperature and body size).
source: This phenotype is particularly impressive given that tentacle numbers in hydras usually vary in a very small range (from 5 to 8 tentacles, depending on temperature and body size) (Shostak, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shostak, 2012.

claim: Tumorous hydras featuring supernumerary tentacles capture more prey than healthy ones, regardless of whether prey is rare or abundant in the environment.
source: Recently, Boutry et al., 2022a demonstrated that tumorous hydras featuring these supernumerary tentacles capture more prey than healthy ones, regardless of whether prey is rare or abundant in the environment.
evidence: Supported by citation to Boutry et al., 2022a.

claim: Wild specimens of H. oligactis developing spontaneous tumors when placed in laboratory conditions do not seem to develop additional tentacles.
source: In contrast, wild specimens of H. oligactis developing spontaneous tumors when placed in laboratory conditions do not seem to develop additional tentacles (Domazet-Lošo et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Domazet-Lošo et al., 2014.

claim: Food intake, survival, and budding rate are usually positively correlated in hydras.
source: Since food intake, survival, as well as budding rate are usually positively correlated in hydras (Tökölyi et al., 2016), the presence of additional tentacles in certain tumorous hydras is likely to have an adaptive value, favoring host survival despite the cost of bearing tumors, and this can ultimately enhance the hydra's reproductive potential and/or the tumor cells' transmission (see also Boutry et al., 2022b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tökölyi et al., 2016.

claim: The presence of additional tentacles in certain tumorous hydras is likely to have an adaptive value, favoring host survival despite the cost of bearing tumors.
source: Since food intake, survival, as well as budding rate are usually positively correlated in hydras (Tökölyi et al., 2016), the presence of additional tentacles in certain tumorous hydras is likely to have an adaptive value, favoring host survival despite the cost of bearing tumors, and this can ultimately enhance the hydra's reproductive potential and/or the tumor cells' transmission (see also Boutry et al., 2022b).
evidence: Based on inference from the correlation between food intake, survival, and budding rate, and citation to Boutry et al., 2022b.

claim: Additional tentacles can ultimately enhance the hydra's reproductive potential and/or the tumor cells' transmission.
source: Since food intake, survival, as well as budding rate are usually positively correlated in hydras (Tökölyi et al., 2016), the presence of additional tentacles in certain tumorous hydras is likely to have an adaptive value, favoring host survival despite the cost of bearing tumors, and this can ultimately enhance the hydra's reproductive potential and/or the tumor cells' transmission (see also Boutry et al., 2022b).
evidence: Based on inference from the correlation between food intake, survival, and budding rate, and citation to Boutry et al., 2022b.

claim: Healthy hydras grafted with tumorous tissue have an increased risk to subsequently develop tumors compared to those grafted with healthy tissue.
source: On average, healthy hydras grafted with tumorous tissue, either from the transmissible or the spontaneous tumors, have an increased risk to subsequently develop tumors compared to those grafted with healthy tissue (Figure 3, pie charts).
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3 pie charts.

claim: Hydras grafted with transmissible tumors developed on average eight times more tumors than those transplanted with healthy tissue (IRR=8.00 [2.73–23.49], p<0.001).
source: Hydras grafted with transmissible tumors developed on average eight times more tumors (incidence rate ratio [IRR]=8.00 [2.73–23.49], p<0.001) than those transplanted with healthy tissue, whereas for spontaneous tumor transplants the risk only increased 2.61 times (IRR = 2.61 [1.09–6.23], p=0.031).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis showing IRR and p<0.001.

claim: For spontaneous tumor transplants the risk of tumor development increased 2.61 times (IRR = 2.61 [1.09–6.23], p=0.031).
source: Hydras grafted with transmissible tumors developed on average eight times more tumors (incidence rate ratio [IRR]=8.00 [2.73–23.49], p<0.001) than those transplanted with healthy tissue, whereas for spontaneous tumor transplants the risk only increased 2.61 times (IRR = 2.61 [1.09–6.23], p=0.031).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis showing IRR and p=0.031.

claim: Hydra grafted with healthy tissues also developed tumors but at lower, yet non-negligible, rate compared to hydra grafted with tumorous tissues.
source: However, an intriguing result is that hydra grafted with healthy tissues also developed tumors but at lower, yet non-negligible, rate compared to hydra grafted with tumorous tissues (Figure 3, pie charts; 48.75, 48.12, and 28.92%, on average, for healthy tissues from Mt, Spb, and Rob, respectively).
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3 with specific percentages.

claim: Individuals transplanted with tissue from transmitted tumors showed a significant increase in the number of tentacles.
source: The number of tentacles (Figure 3A, dot plots) showed a significant increase in individuals transplanted with tissue from transmitted tumors (even if the effect remains low when the donor is Rob and the recipient is SpB), whereas there was no significant effect in individuals transplanted with tissues from spontaneous tumors (Figure 3B and C, dot plots), relative to individuals transplanted with healthy tissue.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3A dot plots.

claim: There was no significant effect on tentacle number in individuals transplanted with tissues from spontaneous tumors relative to individuals transplanted with healthy tissue.
source: The number of tentacles (Figure 3A, dot plots) showed a significant increase in individuals transplanted with tissue from transmitted tumors (even if the effect remains low when the donor is Rob and the recipient is SpB), whereas there was no significant effect in individuals transplanted with tissues from spontaneous tumors (Figure 3B and C, dot plots), relative to individuals transplanted with healthy tissue.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3B and C dot plots.

claim: An individual transplanted with transmitted tumor tissues developed 1.45 [1.21–1.73] additional tentacles on average while individuals transplanted with healthy tissue developed only one additional tentacle (IRR = 1.45 [1.21–1.73], p<0.001).
source: On average, an individual transplanted with transmitted tumor tissues developed 1.45 [1.21–1.73] additional tentacles while individuals transplanted with healthy tissue developed only one additional tentacle (IRR = 1.45 [1.21–1.73], p<0.001), with no significant effect of the donor lineage.
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis showing IRR and p<0.001.

claim: When the recipient already had a relatively high number of tentacles, the increase in the number of tentacles after transplantation was reduced (IRR = 0.82 [0.74–0.92], p=0.001).
source: Furthermore, we also detected a negative effect of the initial number of tentacles of the recipient (Figure 3, dot plots): when the recipient already had a relatively high number of tentacles, the increase in the number of tentacles after transplantation was reduced (IRR = 0.82 [0.74–0.92], p=0.001), highlighting a possible threshold effect.
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis showing IRR and p=0.001.

claim: The number of buds produced per individual during the 10 weeks of the study was significantly correlated with the number of supernumerary tentacles developed by the individual during the same period.
source: Regardless of the type of donor and recipient, the number of buds produced per individual during the 10 weeks of the study was found to be significantly correlated with the number of supernumerary tentacles developed by the individual during the same period (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4.

claim: The slope of the correlation between bud production and supernumerary tentacles was notably reduced for hydras with tumors (n=92, estimate = –2.75 [–5.21–0.29], p=0.029).
source: However, the slope of this correlation was notably reduced for hydras with tumors (Figure 4, n=92, estimate = –2.75 [–5.21–0.29], p=0.029).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis showing estimate and p=0.029.

claim: An individual developing a tumor will require more supplementary tentacles than a healthy individual to achieve the same number of buds produced.
source: Consequently, all other factors being equal, an individual developing a tumor will require more supplementary tentacles than a healthy individual to achieve the same number of buds produced.
evidence: Based on inference from the reduced slope of correlation between bud production and tentacles in tumorous hydras.

claim: The impact of the number of tentacles and tumor development on the number of buds produced became statistically detectable only after the seventh week of the experiment.
source: Noticeably, we observed that the impact of the number of tentacles and tumor development on the number of buds produced became statistically detectable only after the seventh week of the experiment.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations over time.

claim: This is the first evidence of transmissible tumor cells that have evolved the ability to manipulate an external phenotypic trait in their host.
source: Thus, although the exact mechanisms promoting the growth of additional tentacles remain to be identified, this is the first evidence of transmissible tumor cells that have evolved the ability to manipulate an external phenotypic trait in their host.
evidence: Based on the experimental results showing that transmissible tumors induce tentacle growth.

claim: Both the SpB and Rob tumors were able to trigger supernumerary tentacles in their new hosts.
source: Indeed, both the SpB and Rob tumors were able to trigger supernumerary tentacles in their new hosts, even if Rob microbiome is the same between tumorous and non-tumorous hydras (Domazet-Lošo et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from transplantation experiments and citation to Domazet-Lošo et al., 2014.

claim: Rob microbiome is the same between tumorous and non-tumorous hydras.
source: Indeed, both the SpB and Rob tumors were able to trigger supernumerary tentacles in their new hosts, even if Rob microbiome is the same between tumorous and non-tumorous hydras (Domazet-Lošo et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Domazet-Lošo et al., 2014.

claim: The growth of supernumerary tentacles is induced only by the presence of transmissible tumor cells.
source: While it seems clear that the growth of supernumerary tentacles is induced only by the presence of transmissible tumor cells, to argue for host manipulation in the strict sense (as observed in the case of manipulative parasites; see Ewald, 1980; Poulin, 2010) it is necessary to demonstrate that this phenotypic change is indeed associated with an increase in tumor transmission.
evidence: Based on experimental results showing only transmissible tumors induce tentacle growth.

claim: Tumors impose a cost on the reproductive potential of the host in terms of weaker budding of tumoral individuals.
source: Our results support the hypothesis that tumors do indeed impose a cost on the reproductive potential of the host in terms of the weaker budding of tumoral individuals, but that this cost can be offset by the growth of supernumerary tentacles.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing reduced budding in tumorous individuals.

claim: The cost of tumors on budding can be offset by the growth of supernumerary tentacles.
source: Our results support the hypothesis that tumors do indeed impose a cost on the reproductive potential of the host in terms of the weaker budding of tumoral individuals, but that this cost can be offset by the growth of supernumerary tentacles.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing correlation between tentacle number and bud production.

claim: The supernumerary growth of tentacles can sometimes lead to a significant increase in the number of buds beyond the values presented by healthy individuals with a normal number of tentacles.
source: Beyond this first conclusion, our data also support the hypothesis that the supernumerary growth of tentacles can sometimes not only compensate for the cost of the tumor, but also leads for some cancerous individuals to a significant increase in the number of buds, beyond the values presented by healthy individuals with a normal number of tentacles.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing overcompensation in some tumorous individuals.

claim: The transmission rate of tumors remains constant regardless of the budding rate.
source: Given that the transmission rate of tumors remains constant regardless of the budding rate (Boutry et al., 2022b), all our results thus suggest that tumor-induced supernumerary tentacle growth has likely evolved as an adaptation that enhances their transmission.
evidence: Supported by citation to Boutry et al., 2022b.

claim: Tumor-induced supernumerary tentacle growth has likely evolved as an adaptation that enhances tumor transmission.
source: Given that the transmission rate of tumors remains constant regardless of the budding rate (Boutry et al., 2022b), all our results thus suggest that tumor-induced supernumerary tentacle growth has likely evolved as an adaptation that enhances their transmission.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data and citation to Boutry et al., 2022b.

claim: In H. oligactis new tumors can develop following injury and/or transplantation of healthy tissue alone.
source: An intriguing finding from the present study is that in H. oligactis new tumors can develop following injury and/or transplantation of healthy tissue alone.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations from the transplantation experiments.

claim: Only transmissible tumors are able to consistently alter and increase the number of tentacles in the transplanted individuals.
source: In any case, despite the appearance of spontaneous tumors even after transplantation of healthy tissue, it is striking that only transmissible tumors are able to consistently alter and increase the number of tentacles in the transplanted individuals, which ultimately reinforces our conclusions.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from transplantation experiments.

claim: The St. Petersburg (SpB) and the Robusta (Rob) strains were obtained from Thomas Bosch's laboratory in Kiel.
source: The St. Petersburg (named thereafter SpB) and the Robusta (named thereafter Rob) strains were obtained from Thomas Bosch's laboratory in Kiel (Domazet-Lošo et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Domazet-Lošo et al., 2014.

claim: Control lines for SpB and Rob were isolated from healthy polyps collected during the same sampling and are supposed to be genetically identical to their respective tumorous lines.
source: For each of these two lines, control lines were also isolated from healthy polyps collected during the same sampling; these control groups do not harbor any sign of transmitted tumors and are supposed to be genetically identical to their respective tumorous lines (Boutry et al., 2022b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Boutry et al., 2022b.

claim: The Montaud (Mt) lineage was isolated from a polyp sampled in Montaud water pond and maintained in the lab since August 2021.
source: A third tumorous lineage has been recently established in Frédéric Thomas's laboratory in France and was isolated from a polyp sampled in Montaud water pond (43.748211°N, 3.989871°E); this lineage, named Montaud (thereafter Mt), was maintained in the lab since August 2021 (Boutry et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Boutry et al., 2023.

claim: Tumors from the SpB and Rob tumorous hydra lineages have been vertically transmitted through budding for 15 years.
source: 'Transmitted tumors' correspond to those from the tumorous hydra lineages (SpB and Rob) obtained from Thomas Bosch's laboratory in Kiel; hydras bearing these tumors possess an enhanced number of tentacles and these tumors have been vertically transmitted through budding for 15 years (Lange, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lange, 2010.

claim: Tumors were never observed to appear spontaneously in the Rob control lineage.
source: Noticeably, tumors were never observed to appear spontaneously in the Rob control lineage.
evidence: Stated as an observation from the study.

claim: The period of 3 days was assumed to be sufficient time to allow tumor cells to migrate into the tissue before graft removal.
source: Three days later, the protrusion created by the graft was excised using a scalpel blade, allowing the individual to return to a normal morphology. The period of 3 days was assumed to be sufficient time to allow tumor cells to migrate into the tissue before graft removal (Domazet-Lošo et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Domazet-Lošo et al., 2014.

claim: This is the first evidence that, like true parasites, transmissible tumors can evolve strategies to manipulate the phenotype of their host.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first evidence that, like true parasites, transmissible tumors can evolve strategies to manipulate the phenotype of their host.
evidence: Based on the experimental results showing transmissible tumors induce tentacle growth that enhances transmission.

claim: Supernumerary tentacles permit higher foraging efficiency for the host.
source: Also, supernumerary tentacles, by permitting higher foraging efficiency for the host, were associated with an increased budding rate, thereby favoring the vertical transmission of tumors.
evidence: Based on inference from previous work showing tumorous hydras with supernumerary tentacles capture more prey.

claim: Supernumerary tentacles were associated with an increased budding rate, thereby favoring the vertical transmission of tumors.
source: Also, supernumerary tentacles, by permitting higher foraging efficiency for the host, were associated with an increased budding rate, thereby favoring the vertical transmission of tumors.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing correlation between tentacle number and bud production.

claim: Only the long-term transmissible tumors were able to trigger the growth of additional tentacles.
source: By experimentally transplanting healthy as well as neoplastic tissues derived from both recent and long-term transmissible tumors, we found that only the long-term transmissible tumors were able to trigger the growth of additional tentacles.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from transplantation experiments.
